name: Primates
oneLiner: A dead classifieds monolith rewritten as seven .NET 9 services with Aspire and tag-driven deployment to Fly.io.
summary: The old classifieds monolith (FSE) was rewritten from scratch as seven ASP.NET Core services: identity with RS256 and JWKS, adverts with a taxonomy and publication broken into five steps, an append-only points ledger, stateless media, chat over Claude, and an ephemeral promotion-expiry job. Aspire composes it locally; production is Fly.io. The most interesting decision is not the split but the way the domain was recovered from the legacy code: entities in three services were not rewritten by hand but generated by a parser over the EF snapshot, and `tools/verify-model-usage.py` checks that every property used in fluent configuration, in LINQ and in initialisers actually exists on the entity. The script caught four real defects, among them an index on the non-existent column `AdvertTraffic` and an `IsActive` flag that is not in the schema. The shared {{term:servicedefaults|ServiceDefaults}} kernel has a mechanical ceiling of 800 lines enforced in CI (542 today) plus architecture tests that block entities and `DbContext` from entering it. The documentation is stronger here than the code: 14 ADRs, a register of deviations, and an audit that gives itself a score of 22 items out of 103.
license: brak pliku LICENSE w repozytorium; `src/Primates.Web/package.json` deklaruje MIT, ale to metadana odziedziczona po legacy aplikacji Angulara
tests: One test project: `tests/Primates.ArchitectureTests` with 2 [Fact] attributes and 1 [Theory] over 4 rows of InlineData, so 6 cases, all about the ADR-002 rules for {{term:kernel|the shared kernel}}; the 23 `.spec.ts` files in the Angular app are CLI-generated 'should create' stubs that CI does not run, and the points ledger, the publication pipeline and both frontends have not a single test.
ci: Five workflows. `flyio.yml` (35 KB) is the backbone: {{term:tagdeploy|triggered by a `v*` tag}}, a test gate (kernel-size-check, Release build, dotnet test), change detection against the previous tag, a build matrix pushing to `registry.fly.io`, and deployment in dependency order with verification of the JWKS endpoint. The rest are manual scale/destroy, publishing `docs/index.html` to Pages, and a manual PDF build of the business analysis from LaTeX; there is no secret scanner in any of them.

metrics.label: Projects in the solution
metrics.value: 11 .NET projects in `Primates.sln` (10 in `src/`, 1 in `tests/`); the Angular `src/Primates.Web` has no project file and is not in the solution

metrics.label: .razor pages in BlazorWeb
metrics.value: 18 `.razor` files with an `@page` directive (20 routes); 26 is the count of all `.razor` files

components.name: Primates.ServiceDefaults
components.description: Six files and 542 lines of cross-cutting plumbing and nothing else: {{term:otel|OpenTelemetry}}, health checks, service discovery, HTTP resilience, JWT validation with an optional second issuer, a provider-portable EF setup and a SQL script runner. It holds not one entity and no `DbContext`, and the architecture tests keep it that way.

components.name: Testy architektoniczne + kernel-size-check.sh
components.description: xunit checks that the kernel assembly contains no entity types, no `DbContext` subclasses and no types with domain names (Seed, Constants, Pricing, Promotion), and a bash script fails CI above 800 lines. The rule is neutral about the domain and moves to another repository by changing a path and a base type name.

components.name: Generator encji i weryfikator modelu
components.description: Three Python scripts working on the syntax of the EF Core snapshot rather than on the domain: a snapshot parser, an entity class generator and `verify-model-usage.py`, which confronts every property used in the code with the schema. It will work for any migration of a legacy EF schema onto new entities.

components.name: Pipeline deployu na Fly.io
components.description: {{term:tagdeploy|Tag-driven}} deployment with change detection against the previous tag, a 'no application on Fly = always build' rule for a cold environment, build-once-deploy-many through `registry.fly.io` and an ordered sequence of services. The variables are application names and Dockerfile paths; the mechanism is independent of the domain.

components.name: Primates.AgentService
components.description: Stateless chat over Claude in which the agent has no capability beyond the logged-in user: the five tools are thin wrappers over already authorised adverts and billing endpoints, called with the user's token through `BearerTokenForwardingHandler`. Tools that spend points pause the turn and wait for explicit confirmation, and the loop has a limit of 8 iterations.

components.name: Primates.BlazorWeb
components.description: A second frontend built to the BFF pattern (ADR-014): the browser talks only to its own origin, tokens sit in a server-side cookie session, images go through its own `/media/{id}`. 18 routable pages (`.razor` files with `@page`, 20 routes in total) out of 26 `.razor` files in the project, including paid contact unlocking and the agent chat UI, which Angular never delivered.

components.name: Primates.AdvertsService
components.description: The largest service, 26 entities: the taxonomy of marketplaces and categories, search, dynamic forms, moderation, and advert publication broken into a pipeline of five steps in place of the legacy god-service. The `ApplyAttributesStep` step still does not save attributes, and the documentation admits it.

components.name: Primates.BillingService
components.description: An append-only points ledger with a serialisable spend transaction, pricing that depends on the marketplace, the category, the transaction type and promotions, plus a mock payment provider behind an `IPaymentProvider` interface. The ledger pattern is general; the implementation is tied to the `AdvertCost` type.

overlaps.reason: The AppHost runs the image `ghcr.io/konradcinkusz/authservice:v0.3.1` as a second token issuer (ADR-013), and its own IdentityService stays as a compatibility path. It is the only consumer that stood that service next to an existing identity rather than in its place.
The whole repository is measured against the P1-P15 checklist from there, and `docs/architecture/07-STANDARDS-FEEDBACK.md` returns corrections to the standard itself. The coupling runs both ways.
AgentService is another agent over Claude with tools and a confirmation gate, so the same class of problem as tooling for running agents.

product: No buyer. This is not a sellable product but a reference implementation of the estate standards on a real, ugly domain inherited from a dead monolith. The value is twofold: evidence of migration competence (seven services, JWKS, tag-driven deployment, its own compliance audit) and a testing ground from which rules later travel to architecture-standards and authservice. The business analysis and ADR-011 describe a revenue model for the portal in the form of points and a Pro subscription, but no paying user exists and nothing in the repository suggests otherwise.
gaps: **CI deploys neither BlazorWeb nor authservice.** The files `flyio/blazorweb.fly.toml` and `flyio/authservice.fly.toml` exist, but the words 'blazor' and 'authservice' do not appear in `.github/workflows/flyio.yml` even once, and the SERVICES array in detect-changes does not contain them. The second frontend and the new token issuer have no path to production.
There are no tests outside the kernel. The six cases are about the ADR-002 rules; item 16 of the standards checklist is red for all seven deployables and the documentation records this itself.

**Zero git tags in this clone, with deployment triggered only by a `v*` tag.** From the repository there is no way to confirm that any release actually went out, and the `primates-*.fly.dev` addresses come from the `app=` lines in fly.toml and from `docs/deployment.md`, not from a query. The history contains fixes for deployment errors, so something was being run, but that is circumstantial.

{{term:otel|OTLP}} export is wired into the kernel, and no fly.toml sets `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`. The deployed environment exports telemetry nowhere, and item 4 of the standards audit says so outright.

Seven of the eight Dockerfiles have `org.opencontainers.image.source` pointing at `konradcinkusz/FSE`, a source that no longer exists; only `src/Primates.AgentService/Dockerfile` points at `konradcinkusz/primates`. The images in registry.fly.io sign themselves with a repository that is not there.
next: Add BlazorWeb and authservice deployment to `flyio.yml`, or delete their fly.toml files. The current state promises a deployment that does not exist.
Move the Google Maps key out of four Angular modules into the existing `assets/config.json` and add gitleaks to the workflow. The key is in the history, so rotation is necessary anyway.
Add a LICENSE file and correct `org.opencontainers.image.source` in seven Dockerfiles to point at this repository.
Push a `v*` tag and confirm that the cold-environment rule really does bring the whole estate up from nothing. Today that is a promise untested from the repository.
Write characterisation tests for the points ledger and the publication pipeline before anything in them changes.
highlights: The shared {{term:kernel|kernel}} has a **mechanical ceiling**: `kernel-size-check.sh` fails CI above 800 lines (542 today), and `SharedKernelTests.cs` blocks entities, `DbContext` and types with domain names from entering. The same rule has already failed twice in this estate when it was only written down in a document.

The entities were not rewritten by hand but generated by a parser over the EF snapshot, and `verify-model-usage.py` caught **four real defects**, among them an index on the non-existent column `AdvertTraffic` and an `IsActive` flag that the schema does not contain.

The cold-environment rule in the deployment: a service whose application on Fly does not yet exist is always selected for the build, so the whole environment comes up from the first tag without a manual `fly launch`. The deployment order verifies the JWKS endpoint before the rest starts.

`docs/BUSINESS-ANALYSIS-COVERAGE.md` is an audit of its own code against 103 business analysis requirements, citing files and lines, ending in a verdict of **22 done / 52 partial / 29 missing**. A document that gives itself a bad mark.

The agent over Claude has no capability beyond the logged-in user: the five tools are wrappers over authorised endpoints called with his token, and every tool that spends points pauses the turn and waits for explicit confirmation.
risks: **A committed Google Maps API key** in four Angular modules and no secret scanner in any workflow, even though phase 0 of its own migration plan requires one. The key is in the git history, so rotation is the only real remedy. The key prefix has been removed from this entry, because this entry is public.

No LICENSE file, in a repository cited from other repositories in the estate; the Angular `package.json` declares MIT, which is metadata inherited from the legacy code and can be read as the licence for the whole thing.

Two token issuers run in parallel deliberately (`Jwt:AdditionalAuthority`), but an account created in authservice is a different principal from the same account in IdentityService. ADR-013 admits that there is no continuity of the user identifier.

Angular 10 with ngcc, rxjs-compat and core-js 2.5.1 is an abandoned dependency chain with no security support. 169 TS files stay in the repository with no decision about what to do with them, and some admin screens call four `/Admin/*` endpoints that the backend does not have.
headline: Documentation audits its own code at 22/103; no tests outside the kernel
